paragraphs: An agent facing an unfamiliar situation may need help with more than a single answer or action. This paper studies how an agent can learn to request useful information from an assistant who understands its task and environment. The central problem is making assistance part of the agent’s decision process, including interpreting what the assistant provides.

The proposed interactive framework supports rich information whose usefulness depends on context. Its practical demonstration involves navigation with simulated human assistance. The agent learns an assistance-requesting policy, allowing it to take advantage of different kinds of information in different situations. The authors also examine assistants that can recursively break a task into smaller subtasks.

In previously unseen navigation environments, the assisted agent achieves up to seven times the success rate of fully autonomous behavior. That is a reported maximum improvement in the studied setting. The work also analyzes benefits and challenges of learning to ask for help when task decomposition is available, connecting assistance quality with the structure of the task.
icml-2022-a-framework-for-learning-to-re.tldr: A learned assistance-requesting policy helps navigation agents use contextually useful guidance, with up to sevenfold success-rate improvements in unseen environments.

paragraphs: Causal definitions of fairness specify which cause-and-effect relationships a decision system should constrain. This paper organizes popular definitions into two families: those restricting how decisions affect counterfactual disparities, and those restricting how protected characteristics affect decisions. It then asks what happens when these definitions become requirements for choosing a policy.

The authors find analytically and empirically that both families almost always produce strongly Pareto dominated policies, in a measure-theoretic sense. Here, domination means that an unconstrained alternative is preferred by every stakeholder whose preferences belong to a specified broad, natural class. The qualification about preferences matters: the result is framed around that class, rather than every imaginable view of fairness.

For college admissions, the relevant stakeholders have neutral or positive preferences for academic preparedness and diversity. Under one prominent fairness definition, the authors prove that admissions must assign every student the same probability, regardless of qualifications or group. These findings identify formal limitations and potentially adverse consequences of the studied causal constraints, showing why a mathematically defined fairness requirement needs scrutiny of its resulting decisions.
icml-2022-causal-conceptions-of-fairness.tldr: Common causal fairness constraints can yield policies that every stakeholder within a broad specified preference class would prefer to replace.

paragraphs: Adversarial purification uses a generative model to remove malicious changes from an input before classification. This approach can protect an existing classifier without assuming a particular attack form or classifier architecture. The paper introduces DiffPure to improve purification performance, which the authors describe as previously trailing defenses based on adversarial training.

DiffPure first adds a small amount of noise to an adversarial image through a forward diffusion process. It then applies the reverse generative process to recover a clean image. The defense therefore relies on a controlled noising-and-recovery procedure. For evaluation against strong adaptive attacks, the authors use an adjoint method to compute full gradients through the reverse process efficiently and at scale.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA-HQ, together with ResNet, WideResNet, and vision transformer classifiers. In these evaluations, DiffPure achieves state-of-the-art results and exceeds existing adversarial training and purification methods, often substantially. The findings support diffusion-based purification across the tested datasets and architectures, while the adaptive-attack procedure provides a way to assess attacks that account for the defense.
icml-2022-diffusion-models-for-adversari.tldr: DiffPure uses diffusion-based image recovery to remove adversarial perturbations and outperforms existing defenses in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A single demonstration of an object rearrangement task can support several interpretations of the intended goal. An agent may reproduce the demonstrated arrangement yet fail when the environment changes because it inferred the wrong spatial requirements. This paper addresses that ambiguity by learning goal representations intended to carry across environments.

Graph-based Equivalence Mappings, or GEM, represents a goal through a reward function conditioned on two components. A graph identifies important spatial relationships between objects, while mappings attached to its edges describe properties of those relationships that remain invariant. This separates which relationships matter from which changes preserve them, providing structure for learning a transferable goal.

GEM combines inverse reinforcement learning with active reward learning to refine the reward function. It uses the graph structure and domain randomization enabled by the equivalence mappings to support that refinement. Experiments with simulated oracles and human participants show that GEM can substantially improve generalization over strong baselines. The result concerns learning the intended spatial specification from ambiguous evidence, making the representation of the goal central to successful imitation.
icml-2022-discovering-generalizable-spat.tldr: GEM learns graph-structured spatial goals from a demonstration and active feedback, improving object-rearrangement generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor regression predicts a target by averaging the targets of nearby examples. Its success depends on what counts as nearby: irrelevant features can distort neighbor selection. Averaging also overlooks how the target function changes around those examples. Differential Nearest Neighbors Regression, or DNNR, addresses both problems through estimates of local change.

During training, DNNR estimates local gradients and uses them to scale features. During prediction, it uses estimated gradients in an nth-order Taylor approximation, incorporating local function behavior into the prediction. The same general idea therefore informs both the geometry used to find neighbors and the calculation made from those neighbors.

Across more than 250 datasets, the authors report performance comparable to state-of-the-art gradient boosting methods and multilayer perceptrons. They also retain the simplicity and transparency associated with nearest-neighbor methods, which enables theoretical error bounds and examination of failures. The contribution is a way to strengthen a familiar, inspectable regression approach while preserving a connection between predictions and local data behavior.
icml-2022-dnnr-differential-nearest-neig.tldr: DNNR uses local gradient estimates to improve neighbor selection and prediction, matching strong regression methods across more than 250 datasets.

paragraphs: Designing a robotic swimmer requires modeling how its deforming body and the surrounding fluid affect each other. Fully coupled simulations are expensive, and gradient-free optimization adds further computational work. This paper develops a differentiable hybrid simulator that combines direct simulation of the swimmer’s structure with a learned approximation of fluid behavior.

The structural component is a two-dimensional deformable-body simulation using computer graphics techniques to accelerate the finite-element method. The fluid component uses a U-Net trained with a physics-based loss to predict the flow field at each time step. An immersed boundary method samples predicted pressure and velocity around the swimmer’s boundary to calculate its motion.

The authors demonstrate computational efficiency and differentiability on a two-dimensional carangiform swimmer. Differentiability matters because gradients can guide optimization of controls for soft bodies moving through fluids, avoiding reliance on gradient-free searches for that purpose. The stated demonstration is two-dimensional, and the contribution combines faster simulation with a direct route from simulated motion back to the control choices being optimized.
icml-2022-fast-aquatic-swimmer-optimizat.tldr: A differentiable hybrid simulator combines deformable-body physics and learned fluid dynamics to support faster, gradient-based swimmer control optimization.

paragraphs: This paper investigates diffusion models that generate images from text descriptions. Guidance is a central design choice because it can trade image diversity for fidelity. The authors compare CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance, asking which produces images that people judge as more photorealistic and better matched to their captions.

Human evaluators prefer classifier-free guidance on both criteria, and the resulting samples are often photorealistic. Evaluators also favor samples from the authors’ 3.5-billion-parameter text-conditioned model over samples from DALL-E, even when DALL-E uses expensive CLIP reranking. These are comparative human judgments from the reported evaluation, supporting the particular guidance choice and model studied.

The work also shows that the models can be fine-tuned for image inpainting, enabling text-directed editing of images. This extends the approach from producing an image to modifying image content through textual instructions. The authors additionally train and release a smaller model on filtered data, so the released model is distinguished from the larger model used in the highlighted comparison.
icml-2022-glide-towards-photorealistic-i.tldr: GLIDE finds strong human preference for classifier-free text-guided diffusion and extends the approach to text-driven image editing.

paragraphs: When a learning problem has more flexibility than the data can uniquely determine, the training procedure influences which solution is selected. This preference is called implicit bias. The paper uses diagonal linear networks to investigate how gradient descent’s step size can change that preference and, consequently, the ability to generalize.

For non-centered data, the authors show that large steps can move learning from a kernel-like regime to a rich regime that favors sparse predictors. This shift can occur even when gradient flow, the continuous-time training model considered in earlier work, would remain in the kernel regime. Step size can therefore alter the kind of solution learned, beyond simply changing training speed.

The argument uses dynamic stability. Convergence to dynamically stable global minima implies a bound on a weighted sum of predictor coefficient magnitudes, expressed as a weighted l1 norm. That bound characterizes the sparsity-inducing regime. The authors then prove good generalization in a sparse regression setting, linking the optimization behavior to a concrete setting where a preference for sparsity is useful.
icml-2022-implicit-bias-of-the-step-size.tldr: Large gradient descent steps can induce sparsity-favoring behavior in diagonal linear networks, with proven generalization benefits in a sparse regression setting.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with sensitive data must balance learning effective behavior against protecting the data used during exploration. This paper studies that problem under joint differential privacy in linear Markov decision processes, where both rewards and dynamics have linear structure. Performance is measured through regret, the accumulated cost of learning instead of acting optimally.

The proposed algorithm improves the dependence of regret on the number of episodes K from K to the three-fifths power to the optimal square-root dependence. Its key choice is an adaptive policy-update schedule: the policy changes only when the data have changed sufficiently. This produces only logarithmically many updates in K and greatly reduces the privacy noise needed.

Fewer policy changes also give the algorithm a low switching cost. When the privacy parameter epsilon is constant, the additional regret caused by privacy appears only in lower-order terms relative to existing non-private bounds. Under that regime, the result makes the privacy cost negligible in the stated comparison, while retaining an explicit privacy constraint throughout learning.
icml-2022-improved-regret-for-differenti.tldr: Adaptive, infrequent policy updates achieve optimal square-root episode dependence for private exploration in linear MDPs while reducing privacy noise.

paragraphs: An ensemble can improve predictions by combining several neural networks, but running every network is expensive. Ensemble distillation aims to transfer those capabilities into a smaller student. This paper focuses on two connected choices: how to structure the student during learning, and which training inputs best expose the ensemble’s useful diversity.

The proposed student contains multiple subnetworks during training so it can absorb differences in the teachers’ functions. These subnetworks are then appropriately averaged in weight space for inference, producing a single student network without additional inference cost. The training structure gives diversity a role while still yielding one network to run after distillation.

A second component perturbs inputs to find cases where the teachers’ diversity can be transferred more effectively. It complements the student design by changing the information presented during training. Combining the two techniques significantly improves on earlier methods across various image classification tasks. The reported benefit is therefore better ensemble knowledge transfer alongside the deployment cost of a single student.
icml-2022-improving-ensemble-distillatio.tldr: Training diverse student subnetworks with informative perturbed inputs improves ensemble distillation while retaining a single network at inference.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions through a plan for moving mass between them. Computing transport on mini-batches helps with memory demands in large applications, but a locally optimal plan can include matches that disagree with the plan for the full distributions. This paper studies those misspecified mappings and how to reduce them.

The proposed method, mini-batch partial optimal transport, limits the amount of mass transported between mini-batches. Allowing partial transportation relaxes the pressure to match all the available mass within each small comparison. The authors use this perspective to explain the source of incorrect mini-batch mappings and why controlling the transported amount can alleviate the problem.

Experiments assess the method in deep domain adaptation, partial domain adaptation, deep generative modeling, color transfer, and gradient flow. The reported results are favorable relative to current mini-batch methods. The contribution targets the quality of the transport mappings while retaining a mini-batch approach to the memory problem; the claim is that partial transport can reduce incorrect mappings, rather than guarantee recovery of every full-distribution match.
icml-2022-improving-mini-batch-optimal-t.tldr: Restricting how much mass moves between mini-batches can reduce incorrect transport matches and improves results across several reported applications.

paragraphs: Multi-head attention gives transformers multiple ways to attend to their inputs, but attention heads can learn redundant representations. This paper takes that observation as motivation to change what each head contains. Transformer-MGK replaces redundant heads with mixtures of attention keys, allowing individual heads to focus efficiently on different parts of a sequence.

The keys follow a Gaussian mixture model. This provides multiple key components within a head and changes the allocation of attention capacity. Compared with conventional transformer counterparts, the proposed architecture uses fewer parameters and floating-point operations, speeds training and inference, and achieves comparable or better accuracy across the evaluated tasks. It can also be extended to linear attention.

The empirical study includes language modeling and applications with very long sequences. On Wikitext-103 and Long Range Arena, four-head Transformer-MGK models perform comparably to or better than eight-head baseline transformers. These results support probabilistic key mixtures as a way to use attention capacity more efficiently in the tested settings, with computational savings accompanying the prediction results.
icml-2022-improving-transformers-with-pr.tldr: Gaussian mixtures of attention keys let transformers use fewer heads and less computation while maintaining or improving performance in reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: A robustness measurement needs a definition of which input changes should leave a model unaffected. Such definitions commonly rely on human judgments about what counts as a meaningless change. This paper proposes using another neural network as the reference, making robustness a question about how much two networks agree on what can change without mattering.

The resulting measure, STIR, captures shared invariances between networks. An invariance describes a change to which a network is insensitive. STIR adapts existing measures of representation similarity so they can assess this property. Its focus is therefore on agreement about tolerated changes, giving the choice of reference network an explicit role in the assessment.

The authors use STIR to study how shared invariances vary with weight initialization, architecture, loss function, and training dataset. This supplies a framework for investigating which design and training choices influence representational robustness relative to another model. The contribution broadens the reference used to define robustness and provides a measurement tool for examining the resulting relationships between networks.
icml-2022-measuring-representational-rob.tldr: STIR measures representational robustness through the input invariances shared by a network and a chosen reference network.

paragraphs: Training one model for several tasks can save computation and improve data efficiency, but tasks can disagree about how shared parameters should change. Their gradients may conflict, leaving joint training worse than training separate models. This paper focuses on the step that combines those gradients into a single update direction.

The authors formulate that combination as a bargaining game in which the tasks negotiate a shared direction. Under certain assumptions, the game has a unique Nash Bargaining Solution. They use this solution to define Nash-MTL, replacing a heuristic choice of gradient combination with one grounded in the stated bargaining formulation and its assumptions.

The paper develops the resulting optimization procedure and provides theoretical convergence guarantees. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple multi-task benchmarks in different domains. Together, these contributions connect a formal model of agreement between tasks to an operational training method. The uniqueness claim remains conditional on the bargaining assumptions, while the reported benchmark results provide empirical support for using that solution in multi-task optimization.
icml-2022-multi-task-learning-as-a-barga.tldr: Nash-MTL combines task gradients through a bargaining solution, with convergence guarantees and strong reported multi-task benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Mini-batch optimal transport scales distribution comparison by solving smaller transport problems and averaging their costs and plans. However, this procedure ignores relationships between the mini-batches themselves. The paper identifies undesirable estimates and a failure of the identity property, which prevents the usual mini-batch construction from approximating a proper metric in the stated sense.

Batch of Mini-batches Optimal Transport, or BoMb-OT, adds a higher-level transport problem that finds an optimal coupling between mini-batches. This makes the relationships among batches part of the calculation. The authors show that the construction can be understood as an approximation to a well-defined distance between probability measures.

They also connect the new method to the previous approach: ordinary mini-batch optimal transport emerges as the entropically regularized BoMb-OT regularization parameter tends to infinity. Experiments cover deep generative models, domain adaptation, approximate Bayesian computation, color transfer, and gradient flow, reporting good performance across these applications. The work thus combines a more structured batch comparison with a theoretical account of how it relates to existing mini-batch transport.
icml-2022-on-transportation-of-mini-batc.tldr: BoMb-OT optimally couples mini-batches to improve distribution comparison and approximate a well-defined distance between probability measures.

paragraphs: A policy gradient indicates how a decision policy should change to improve performance. Estimating it becomes difficult when the available data come from an unknown behavior policy and new samples from the target policy are unavailable. This paper addresses that offline estimation problem, where conventional approaches can have substantial bias or exponentially large variance.

The proposed double Fitted Policy Gradient algorithm supports arbitrary policy parameterizations, assuming access to a Bellman-complete value function class. For linear value approximation, the authors prove a tight finite-sample error bound controlled by distribution mismatch in feature space. This connects estimation accuracy to how the available data and target policy differ through the chosen features.

The authors also establish asymptotic normality with a precise covariance characterization and statistical optimality through a matching Cramer-Rao lower bound. Experiments examine both gradient estimation and policy optimization with softmax tabular policies and ReLU policy networks. Across the reported metrics, FPG substantially outperforms existing approaches based on importance sampling and variance reduction, complementing the theoretical analysis with empirical comparisons.
icml-2022-optimal-estimation-of-policy-g.tldr: Double fitted iteration estimates policy gradients from offline data, with tight error analysis and statistical optimality results under the stated conditions.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training simulates the restricted numerical precision a network will use. This paper examines a failure mode in which quantized weights repeatedly switch between two available values. The authors show that these oscillations can significantly reduce accuracy, making their behavior an important part of understanding low-precision training.

The analysis identifies two consequences: increased noise during training and incorrectly estimated batch-normalization statistics used at inference. The effects are especially pronounced at four bits or fewer in efficient networks with depth-wise separable layers, including MobileNets and EfficientNets. Examining several existing quantization-aware training algorithms, the authors find that most do not overcome the oscillations.

The proposed remedies are oscillation dampening and iterative weight freezing, two training algorithms designed to address the switching behavior. On ImageNet, they achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for three- and four-bit weight and activation quantization in architectures including MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, and EfficientNet-lite. The work connects a specific training instability to deployment accuracy and shows that directly addressing it improves the reported low-bit results.
icml-2022-overcoming-oscillations-in-qua.tldr: Two methods that address oscillating quantized weights improve low-bit network accuracy by targeting a harmful training instability.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning problems involve partial observability: the agent’s current observation does not provide everything needed for a decision. Meta-learning, robustness, generalization, and temporal credit assignment can all be framed this way. Adding memory through a recurrent architecture offers a general approach, although earlier studies often found it weaker than specialized methods.

This paper revisits that comparison by carefully choosing the architecture and hyperparameters of recurrent model-free reinforcement learning. The authors find that these choices can often produce performance comparable to, and sometimes substantially better than, more sophisticated recent approaches. The study places implementation decisions at the center of assessing the strength of a general baseline.

Across 21 environments associated with six prior specialized methods, the implementation achieves better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance in 18 environments. The authors also release a simple, efficient implementation for future comparisons. These findings establish a strong empirical baseline across the tested problems and show why conclusions about the need for specialization depend on how the recurrent alternative is configured.
icml-2022-recurrent-model-free-rl-can-be.tldr: Carefully configured recurrent model-free reinforcement learning beats specialized comparisons in sample efficiency and final performance on 18 of 21 tested environments.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces a set of plausible targets with finite-sample coverage guarantees under exchangeability, an assumption that the data distribution is unchanged by reordering observations. Its direct computation can be impractical because it requires refitting a prediction model for candidate values of the unknown target. A continuous target can entail infinitely many such fits.

This paper combines conformal prediction with algorithmic stability bounds to construct a prediction set using a single model fit. Stability bounds control how a learning algorithm’s output changes when its data change. Bringing those bounds into the conformal procedure provides a way to avoid the repeated fitting that creates the computational bottleneck.

The authors show that their confidence set retains coverage guarantees and does not require splitting the data. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the tightness of the construction when sample sizes are sufficiently large. The contribution therefore pairs a substantial computational simplification with retained coverage, while the empirical statement about tightness explicitly depends on having enough observations.
icml-2022-stable-conformal-prediction-se.tldr: Algorithmic stability bounds enable conformal prediction sets from one model fit while preserving coverage guarantees and avoiding data splitting.

paragraphs: People rely on systems to compress information into manageable descriptions, but the choice of what to reveal can influence their decisions. This paper studies a system that selectively presents an item’s attributes to a user who decides whether to consume it. The system must be truthful about what it reveals, but may omit other information.

The authors formalize the interaction as a learning problem with strategic behavior. The learning user acts first, and the system responds with a representation chosen to influence that user. Because the representation is a selected subset of truthful attributes, the user must learn functions of sets while accounting for strategic subset selection.

The main result is an algorithm that minimizes error despite these strategic representations. The theoretical analysis also examines the trade-off between the effort needed to learn and susceptibility to manipulation. The work makes selective disclosure part of the learning problem itself: a representation can be factually accurate while still being strategically chosen, so robust decisions must account for how the visible information was selected.
icml-2022-strategic-representation-b8ac2.tldr: The paper develops a learning algorithm for making decisions despite strategically selected representations that reveal only truthful subsets of information.

paragraphs: Signed graphs represent relationships as positive or negative, as in a network of social interactions. This paper studies graphs with a clear structure of polarized communities and asks how to identify an individual vertex’s community without processing the entire graph. That is useful when only a small number of membership answers are needed.

The authors construct a local clustering oracle that reads a small portion of the graph. Under bounded maximum degree and at most logarithmically many communities, both preprocessing and each query take roughly square-root time in the number of vertices, with additional logarithmic factors and polynomial dependence on inverse error tolerance. The oracle correctly classifies a one-minus-epsilon fraction of vertices relative to hidden planted communities.

Extending such oracles from unsigned to signed graphs requires new ideas, including spectral analysis of random walks with signs. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate practical performance. The contribution combines local access with a formal accuracy guarantee under the stated graph conditions, offering a way to answer limited clustering queries without constructing every vertex’s assignment.
icml-2022-sublinear-time-clustering-orac.tldr: A local oracle answers signed-graph community queries in sublinear time with accuracy guarantees under explicit structural assumptions.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents collect experience as they learn, so early observations can shape how they respond to later evidence. This paper identifies a tendency to over-rely on early interactions and overlook useful information encountered afterward. The authors call this primacy bias and connect it to overfitting earlier experience while training on progressively growing datasets.

Through experiments, the paper examines algorithmic features that worsen the bias. It then proposes a simple mechanism: periodically reset part of the agent. The intervention targets the agent’s continuing dependence on early experience, addressing a learning problem that can persist even as useful new evidence becomes available.

The authors apply partial resetting to algorithms in both discrete-action Atari 100k tasks and continuous-action DeepMind Control Suite tasks, consistently improving performance in those evaluations. The findings identify adaptation to later experience as an important issue in deep reinforcement learning and provide a broadly applicable mechanism to address it. The reported improvements span both action settings, supporting the practical relevance of the diagnosed bias.
icml-2022-the-primacy-bias-in-deep-reinf.tldr: Periodically resetting part of an agent reduces overreliance on early experience and improves performance in the reported reinforcement learning experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional mean while protecting each user through differential privacy. Each user may contribute multiple samples, creating a trade-off between recruiting more users and obtaining more observations from each one. The authors design a mechanism with a nearly optimal trade-off between those two resources.

The required user count can be as low as order log(1/delta) divided by epsilon, independent of dimension. That independence applies to users: the samples required per user may still grow polynomially with dimension. This improves on earlier work whose user requirements grew polynomially with dimension, and resolves a previously posed problem about private estimation with few users.

The mechanism also tolerates corruption affecting up to 49 percent of users. Beyond mean estimation, the results yield optimal algorithms for privately learning discrete distributions with few users. Through reductions to private mean estimation, they also apply to stochastic convex optimization and a variant of stochastic gradient descent. The contribution therefore makes scarce user participation compatible with both privacy and substantial corruption tolerance.
icml-2022-tight-and-robust-private-mean-.tldr: Private mean estimation can use a dimension-independent number of users, with a nearly optimal sample trade-off and tolerance of up to 49 percent corrupted users.

paragraphs: Neural Processes learn distributions over functions, allowing them to make predictions with uncertainty across tasks. However, underfitting and frequently intractable likelihoods limit existing variants, particularly for sequential decisions. This paper introduces Transformer Neural Processes, which formulate uncertainty-aware meta-learning as sequence modeling and use an autoregressive likelihood objective for training.

The transformer architecture preserves structural requirements of the problem. Reordering observed data points should not change the inference, while reordering unobserved points should correspondingly reorder their predictions. The authors also provide architectural controls that trade a more expressive decoding distribution against additional computation, making that cost-versus-expressivity choice explicit.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on meta-regression, image completion, contextual multi-armed bandits, and Bayesian optimization, outperforming previous Neural Process variants on the evaluated benchmarks. These tasks connect prediction and uncertainty estimation with downstream decision-making. The contribution is a sequence-based formulation that combines an explicit likelihood objective with the ordering properties the problem requires, supported by results across several types of meta-learning and sequential-decision applications.
icml-2022-transformer-neural-processes-u.tldr: Transformer Neural Processes use structured sequence modeling for uncertainty-aware meta-learning and outperform earlier variants across the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Choosing network depth fixes an important part of a model’s complexity before learning begins. This paper introduces an unbounded depth neural network, a probabilistic model containing an infinite sequence of hidden layers. An unbounded prior governs the truncation depth, the layer from which the model produces its data.

After observing data, the model’s posterior describes uncertainty over both network parameters and truncation depth. The authors approximate this posterior with a variational inference algorithm that has no preset upper limit on depth. Its specially structured variational family creates or removes free parameters as the depth distribution is optimized, allowing exploration of truncations entirely through gradient-based optimization.

Experiments on real and synthetic data find that posterior depth adapts to dataset complexity. The model outperforms standard neural networks with similar computational complexity and other approaches to infinite-depth networks in those studies. The contribution treats depth as an inferred quantity alongside weights, providing a gradient-based mechanism for adapting model complexity while representing uncertainty about where the network should be truncated.
icml-2022-variational-inference-for-infi.tldr: An unbounded-depth probabilistic network learns a distribution over its depth through variational inference and adapts complexity to the data.
